why.correct: A hormone built from cholesterol is a steroid, and steroids are lipid-soluble. It diffuses through the phospholipid bilayer, so its receptor protein can sit inside the cell, in the cytosol or the nucleus.
options: Membrane receptor proteins serve water-soluble hormones, which cannot cross the bilayer. A steroid crosses it.
Correct. Lipid-soluble hormones bind intracellular receptor proteins.
Secretory vesicles belong to the cell that makes and releases a water-soluble hormone, not to the target cell's receptor machinery.
A carrier protein moves the hormone through the blood. It is not a receptor protein and does not start a response in the target cell.

why.correct: Epinephrine is water-soluble. It binds membrane receptor proteins, and G proteins and cAMP switch on kinases that change proteins the cell already has, within seconds. The steroid is lipid-soluble. It works through an intracellular receptor protein that changes transcription, and making new mRNA and protein takes hours.
options: Both drugs reach the blood quickly; the delay is inside the target cells, not in absorption.
Correct. Changing existing proteins is fast; making new ones is slow.
Steroids have long half-lives because carrier proteins protect them. Fast clearance is a feature of water-soluble hormones such as epinephrine.
Epinephrine does not enter its target cells; it binds a receptor protein on the surface. The steroid crosses the membrane by itself once it leaves its carrier protein.

why.correct: One hour is 60 ÷ 20 = 3 half-lives. 120 → 60 → 30 → 15 units. The fraction left is (1/2)³ = 1/8, and 120 × 1/8 = 15.
options: 40 units comes from dividing by 3, the number of half-lives. Each half-life halves the level instead.
60 units is the level after one half-life (20 minutes), not after three.
Correct. Three halvings: 120, 60, 30, 15.
30 units is the level after two half-lives (40 minutes).

why.correct: Only free hormone leaves the capillaries and binds receptor proteins. Free fraction = 100% − 95% = 5%, and 5% of 200 = 10 units.
options: 190 units is the bound hormone, which cannot leave the blood while it is attached to a carrier protein.
Correct. The free 5%, 10 units, is the active part.
Not all of it is available: the bound hormone is a reservoir, not an active form.
95 is the bound percentage, not an amount in units.

why.correct: The first messenger never enters the cell. Its receptor protein activates a G protein, which activates adenylyl cyclase. Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP from ATP, cAMP activates protein kinase A, and the kinase phosphorylates target proteins, which changes the cell's behavior.

Only free hormone leaves the blood. It crosses the membrane, binds its receptor protein inside the cell, and the complex binds a hormone response element. Transcription changes, and the new mRNA is translated into protein.

cAMP does not bind DNA at a hormone response element. It switches on protein kinase A in the cytosol. Hormone response elements are where the hormone–receptor complexes of lipid-soluble hormones bind.
options: This step is right. A water-soluble hormone binds a receptor protein in the plasma membrane.
This step is right. The activated G protein switches on adenylyl cyclase.
This step is right. Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cAMP, the second messenger.
This is the error. cAMP acts by switching on protein kinase A; binding a hormone response element is how lipid-soluble hormones work.
This step is right. The kinase changes target proteins by phosphorylating them.

why.correct: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP (cAMP), the second messenger that switches on protein kinase A.
options: Correct. cAMP is made from ATP by adenylyl cyclase.
IP3 is a second messenger made by splitting a membrane phospholipid, not from ATP by adenylyl cyclase. It releases calcium.
DAG is the other product of splitting that phospholipid. It stays in the membrane and helps switch on a different kinase.
mRNA is made by transcription, which is how lipid-soluble hormones act. Adenylyl cyclase does not make it.

why.correct: Phosphodiesterase is one of the switches that end the cAMP signal. Blocking it makes the same hormone signal stronger and longer, without any change at the membrane.

variables.name: cAMP in the cell
variables.why: cAMP is still made by adenylyl cyclase, but phosphodiesterase can no longer break it down, so it builds up.

variables.name: Protein kinase A activity
variables.why: More cAMP is available to bind and switch on protein kinase A.

variables.name: Phosphorylated target proteins
variables.why: A more active kinase phosphorylates more of its target proteins.

variables.name: Hormone bound to membrane receptor proteins
variables.why: The drug acts inside the cell. Binding depends on the hormone level and the number of receptor protein molecules, which have not changed.

why.correct: Carrier proteins hold most of a lipid-soluble hormone in an inactive reservoir. Displacing it raises free, active hormone and its effect, and also exposes it to clearance. Over time negative feedback slows the gland and the free level drifts back.

variables.name: Free hormone in the plasma
variables.why: Hormone knocked off the carrier proteins becomes free hormone.

variables.name: Bound hormone in the plasma
variables.why: Less hormone stays attached to the carrier proteins.

variables.name: Effect on target cells
variables.why: Only free hormone can reach target cells and bind their receptor proteins, so more free hormone means a stronger effect.

variables.name: Rate at which the hormone is cleared from the blood
variables.why: Free hormone is exposed to the liver's enzymes and to filtering by the kidneys; bound hormone is shielded, so clearance speeds up.

why.correct: A humoral stimulus is a change in the level of an ion or nutrient in the blood acting directly on the gland. Here the calcium level itself triggers release.
options: A neural stimulus is a nerve signal to the gland, such as sympathetic fibers triggering the adrenal medulla. No nerve is involved here.
A hormonal stimulus is another hormone triggering release. Here the trigger is calcium, an ion, not a hormone.
Permissive describes how two hormones interact at a target cell, not what triggers a gland to secrete.
Correct. A blood ion level acting on the gland is a humoral stimulus.

why.correct: Nerve signals (the adrenal medulla) are neural stimuli, and one hormone triggering another gland (hypothalamus to pituitary, pituitary to thyroid) is a hormonal stimulus. Changes in glucose or calcium in the blood are humoral stimuli.
options: Correct. Nerve fibers trigger release: a neural stimulus.
Glucose is a nutrient in the blood acting on the gland directly: a humoral stimulus.
Correct. One hormone triggering another gland is a hormonal stimulus.
Calcium is an ion in the blood acting on the gland directly: a humoral stimulus.
Correct. The hypothalamus's hormone triggers the pituitary gland: a hormonal stimulus.

why.correct: Hormone X has no effect of its own but lets hormone Y act fully. That is a permissive effect, often caused by X raising the number of Y's receptor proteins or the machinery behind them.
options: Antagonistic hormones push a variable in opposite directions. Here X does not oppose Y; it helps it.
Correct. X is needed for Y's full effect but does nothing alone.
Negative feedback is a loop that reduces a gland's output when a variable overshoots. It does not describe two hormones acting on one target.
Down-regulation would make the cells less responsive, not more.

why.correct: Together they give 60 units, far more than 10 + 15 = 25. Two hormones that both have an effect and together give more than the sum are synergistic.
options: Correct. 60 is more than the 25 you would expect by adding.
An additive result would be 10 + 15 = 25 units. The combined effect is much larger.
Antagonistic hormones push in opposite directions, so together they would give less, not more.
In a permissive interaction, one hormone has no effect alone. Here both have an effect alone.

why.correct: Adenylyl cyclase is the membrane enzyme that an activated G protein switches on. It converts ATP into cAMP.
options: The G protein is the switch just inside the membrane that sits between the receptor protein and this enzyme.
Protein kinase sits further along the pathway, in the cytoplasm, and is switched on by cAMP.
Correct. This membrane enzyme makes cAMP from ATP.
Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down; it is not drawn in this figure.

why.correct: Inside the cell, the lipid-soluble hormone has bound its intracellular receptor protein, forming a hormone–receptor complex (printed on this figure with the words the other way round) that then moves to the DNA.
options: The carrier protein holds the hormone in the blood and is left behind in the capillary.
The hormone response element is a DNA sequence in the nucleus, where the complex binds next.
Correct. The hormone bound to its receptor protein inside the cell forms this complex.
Messenger RNA is made later, when the gene is transcribed.

why.correct: Steroid hormones are lipids made from cholesterol, with four fused carbon rings. Androgens are one group of steroid hormones.
options: Amine hormones are single amino acids, chemically changed.
Peptide hormones are short chains of amino acids.
Protein hormones are longer, folded chains of amino acids.
Correct. Steroids are built from cholesterol.

why.correct: Protein hormones are chains of amino acids. The gut digests them like any dietary protein, so almost none reaches the blood intact. A steroid is a small lipid that is absorbed as it is and then works normally.
options: Protein hormones are water-soluble and dissolve readily in plasma; that is how injected ones travel.
Steroids do need receptor proteins, inside their target cells. They act there, not in the gut.
Carrier proteins bind lipid-soluble hormones and protect them. They do not destroy protein hormones.
Correct. Digestion breaks proteins into amino acids; steroids survive it.

why.correct: A hormone that stays low for a long time leads target cells to add receptor protein molecules (up-regulation). With more receptor proteins, the same amount of hormone gives a bigger response.
options: Correct. More receptor protein molecules make the cells more sensitive.
Nothing in the scenario points to a change in binding in the blood, and the hormone given is the normal form.
Her gland's output is low; the response here is to hormone given from outside.
Down-regulation happens when a hormone stays high, and it makes cells less sensitive, the opposite of what is seen.

why.correct: Lipid-soluble hormones travel mostly bound to carrier proteins: steroids, including androgens, and the thyroid gland's amines. Water-soluble hormones such as epinephrine and peptides dissolve in the plasma.
options: Epinephrine is water-soluble and dissolves in the plasma, which is one reason its half-life is only about two minutes.
Correct. Steroids are lipid-soluble and ride on carrier proteins.
Correct. Androgens are steroids, so they travel bound to carrier proteins.
Peptides are water-soluble and travel dissolved in the plasma.
Correct. These amines are unusually hydrophobic and travel almost entirely bound.

why.correct: A lipid-soluble hormone acts through its hormone–receptor complex binding a hormone response element on DNA. If the complex cannot bind DNA, transcription does not change, and the proteins that carry out the response are not made.
options: Steroid hormones do not use adenylyl cyclase for their main effect. A broken intracellular receptor protein does not reroute the hormone to a membrane pathway.
Crossing the membrane depends on the hormone being lipid-soluble, not on the receptor protein. The hormone still gets in.
Correct. Without DNA binding, the hormone–receptor complex cannot change transcription.
Binding is only the first step. The response comes from the complex changing which genes are transcribed.

why.correct: Androgens (andr- = male, -gen = producing) are steroid hormones that drive male characteristics such as facial hair and a deeper voice. Both sexes make some, in the gonads and the adrenal glands.
options: Androgens are steroids, so they are lipid-soluble and act through intracellular receptor proteins, not cAMP.
Correct. Androgens are a group of steroid hormones.
Carrier proteins transport androgens; they are not androgens themselves.
The amine made from tryptophan is a sleep-related hormone from the brain, not an androgen.

why.correct: The posterior pituitary is the smaller back lobe of the pituitary gland, continuous with the infundibulum. It is nervous tissue made of the axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons.
options: The anterior pituitary is the larger front lobe, glandular epithelium with no nerve connection to the brain.
Correct. The back lobe, joined to the stalk, is the posterior pituitary.
The infundibulum is the stalk that joins the gland to the hypothalamus, not a lobe of the gland.
The hypothalamus is the part of the brain above the stalk, not part of the pituitary gland.

why.correct: The infundibulum is the stalk that hangs the pituitary gland from the hypothalamus. Hypothalamic axons run down it to the posterior pituitary, and the portal veins run down it to the anterior pituitary.
options: The thalamus is higher up, above the hypothalamus, and is not attached to the pituitary gland.
The posterior pituitary is the back lobe at the bottom of the stalk, not the stalk itself.
Correct. The stalk is the infundibulum.
The anterior pituitary is the front lobe at the bottom of the stalk, not the stalk itself.

why.correct: The posterior pituitary stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, both made by neurons in the hypothalamus. All the others are made by the anterior pituitary.
options: Correct. The posterior lobe releases ADH and oxytocin.
GH and prolactin are made by the anterior pituitary.
TSH and ACTH are tropic hormones of the anterior pituitary.
FSH and LH, the gonadotropins, come from the anterior pituitary.

why.correct: Prolactin is held back mainly by dopamine from the hypothalamus. With the portal link cut, dopamine no longer reaches the anterior pituitary, so prolactin release rises. The other anterior pituitary hormones depend on releasing hormones and fall.
options: Correct. Losing dopamine removes the brake on prolactin.
GH depends mainly on GHRH from the hypothalamus, so it falls when the portal link is cut.
TSH depends on TRH, which can no longer reach the anterior pituitary, so it falls.
LH depends on GnRH, which can no longer reach the anterior pituitary, so it falls.

why.correct: This is acromegaly: excess GH after the epiphyseal plates have closed. Bones can still thicken, especially in the hands, feet, jaw and face, but they cannot grow longer. The same excess in childhood, with open plates, causes gigantism.
options: Correct. Closed epiphyseal plates are why excess GH in adults thickens bones instead of lengthening them.
GH, through IGF-1, still acts on adult bone: that is why her jaw and hands have enlarged.
The tumor is described as secreting growth hormone; IGF-1 comes from the liver and tissues in response to it.
High glucose is a side effect of GH's action on fuel use, not the reason her height is unchanged.

why.correct: Water loss raises plasma osmolarity. Hypothalamic osmoreceptors respond by driving both ADH release, which saves water at the kidney, and thirst, which brings in more water. Both are negative feedback.

variables.name: Plasma osmolarity
variables.why: Sweat is more dilute than plasma, so losing it leaves the remaining plasma more concentrated.

variables.name: Firing of hypothalamic osmoreceptors
variables.why: Water leaves the osmoreceptors into the more concentrated plasma; they shrink, ion channels that open as the membrane slackens let positive ions in, and they fire faster.

variables.name: ADH release
variables.why: Osmoreceptors excite the ADH-making neurons, so the posterior pituitary releases more ADH.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: ADH makes the kidney cells insert aquaporins, so more water is pulled back into the blood.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: Osmoreceptors also excite the thirst center in the hypothalamus.

why.correct: Without ADH the kidneys cannot keep water, so the patient passes large volumes of dilute urine. The thirst center, which still works, makes the patient drink enough to keep up.

variables.name: ADH in the blood
variables.why: The neurons that make ADH are gone, so the posterior pituitary has none to release.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Without ADH, the kidney cells have few aquaporins and cannot pull water back, so large volumes of urine flow out.

variables.name: Urine concentration
variables.why: The water that stays in the urine dilutes it.

variables.name: Thirst
variables.why: Losing so much water raises plasma osmolarity, which excites the thirst center.

variables.name: Water intake
variables.why: The intense thirst drives the patient to drink, which keeps plasma osmolarity from rising far.

why.correct: In SIADH, ADH keeps being released even though the plasma is already dilute. The kidneys keep water, so the urine is concentrated and the plasma becomes dilute with a low sodium concentration. Water moves into brain cells, which swell, causing confusion.
options: Diabetes insipidus is the opposite: too little ADH effect, dilute urine and concentrated plasma.
Excess growth hormone thickens bones and raises the glucose in the blood; it does not concentrate the urine and dilute the plasma.
Oxytocin acts on the uterus and breast. It does not control how much water the kidneys keep.
Correct. Too much ADH explains concentrated urine with dilute plasma.

why.correct: If the thyroid gland fails, its hormones fall and long-loop negative feedback is lost. The hypothalamus and anterior pituitary then push harder, so TSH rises high. Low final hormone with high tropic hormone points to the target gland.
options: A shortage of TRH would lower TSH, not raise it.
A failing anterior pituitary would make TSH low, not high.
Correct. The target gland is failing, and TSH is high because feedback has been removed.
The posterior pituitary does not store TSH; it releases ADH and oxytocin.

why.correct: The drug acts like the final hormone of the adrenal axis, so long-loop feedback suppresses CRH and ACTH. Without ACTH driving them, her adrenal glands shrink and make little steroid. Stopping suddenly would leave her with almost none until the axis recovers, so the dose is tapered.
options: The drug suppresses ACTH through negative feedback; it does not raise it.
ACTH comes only from the anterior pituitary; the adrenal glands cannot make it.
ADH is released from the posterior pituitary, and the anterior pituitary does not switch to making it.
Correct. Feedback has switched off the axis above her adrenal glands.

why.correct: Releasing hormones travel through the hypophyseal portal system: into the first network of capillaries, down the portal veins, out of the second network among the anterior pituitary cells, where they bind receptor proteins and trigger release of the pituitary hormone.

Salt raises plasma osmolarity; osmoreceptors shrink and fire; the ADH-making neurons fire and release ADH from their axon terminals in the posterior pituitary; ADH makes kidney cells add aquaporins, so more water is kept and urine volume falls.
The posterior pituitary is reached by axons, not by portal veins. The hypophyseal portal system carries releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary.
options: This step is right. Oxytocin is made in hypothalamic neurons, mostly in the paraventricular nuclei.
This step is right. The hormone travels inside the axons down the stalk.
This is the error. Portal veins serve the anterior pituitary; oxytocin travels down axons to the posterior pituitary.
This step is right. The posterior pituitary stores the hormone in the axon terminals.
This step is right. Nerve impulses trigger exocytosis of the stored hormone.

why.correct: GnRH makes the anterior pituitary release the two gonadotropins, FSH and LH, which act on the ovaries and testes.
options: Correct. FSH and LH are the gonadotropins.
TSH and ACTH are driven by TRH and CRH and act on the thyroid and adrenal glands.
ADH and oxytocin come from the posterior pituitary and are not controlled by GnRH.
GH is driven by GHRH, and IGF-1 comes from the liver and tissues.

why.correct: TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH each drive another endocrine gland: the thyroid gland, the adrenal gland's outer layer, and the gonads. Prolactin acts on the breast's milk-producing glands and ADH on the kidneys and blood vessels, which are not endocrine glands.
options: Correct. TSH drives the thyroid gland.
Correct. ACTH drives the outer layer of the adrenal gland.
Prolactin acts on the milk-producing glands of the breast, which are not endocrine glands.
Correct. FSH drives the gonads.
ADH acts on the kidneys and blood vessels, not on another endocrine gland.
Correct. LH drives the gonads.

why.correct: Most of GH's growth effect runs through IGF-1. IGF-1 makes chondrocytes in the epiphyseal plates divide, the cartilage is then replaced by bone, and the bone lengthens.
options: Osteoclasts break bone down; they do not lengthen it.
GH does not close the plates; they close under other hormones at the end of puberty, after which GH can only thicken bone.
Correct. IGF-1 drives cartilage growth at the epiphyseal plates.
The rise in glucose is a separate fuel effect of GH, not how it lengthens bone.

why.correct: Alcohol suppresses ADH release. With less ADH, the kidney cells have fewer aquaporins, less water returns to the blood, and more urine is made.
options: Thirst makes you drink more; it does not make the kidneys pass more urine.
Oxytocin acts on the uterus and breast, not on the bladder.
More aquaporins would make the kidneys keep more water and pass less urine.
Correct. Less ADH means less water kept by the kidneys.

why.correct: The orange arrow with a minus sign runs from IGF-1, released by the liver, back to the hypothalamus. IGF-1 makes the hypothalamus release the inhibiting hormone (somatostatin) and less GHRH, so GH release falls.
options: GHRH is the hypothalamic hormone that drives GH release; it is released by the hypothalamus, not by the liver.
Correct. IGF-1 from the liver is the feedback signal.
The liver releases glucose too, but in this figure glucose fuels growth; it is not the feedback arrow.
The inhibiting hormone is what the hypothalamus releases in response to the feedback; it does not come from the liver.

why.correct: Hypothalamic neurons release their releasing and inhibiting hormones into the primary capillary plexus, at the top of the infundibulum. Portal veins then carry them down to the secondary plexus in the anterior pituitary.
options: The secondary plexus is where the hormones leave the blood to reach the anterior pituitary cells, the second network, not the first.
The vein leaving the gland carries the anterior pituitary's own hormones out to the body.
The posterior pituitary is drawn only in outline here and is reached by axons, not by the portal system.
Correct. The primary capillary plexus is the first network.

why.correct: Oxytocin binds receptor proteins on uterine smooth muscle, which adds many of them late in pregnancy, and makes it contract more strongly. Normally it does this through a positive feedback loop driven by stretch of the lower uterus.
options: Correct. Oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions.
Oxytocin's main action is on the muscle of the uterus, not on its blood vessels.
Oxytocin makes the uterus contract, not relax.
Milk production is driven by prolactin. Oxytocin moves milk out; it does not make it.

why.correct: Each round of the loop makes the stimulus, stretch, stronger: positive feedback. It stops when the baby is delivered and the lower uterus is no longer stretched.
options: The loop amplifies the change instead of reversing it, so it is not negative feedback, and oxytocin does not simply run out.
The loop drives contractions stronger; it does not oppose them, so it is not negative feedback.
Correct. Positive feedback, which ends when its stimulus is removed by birth.
ADH has no role in ending the labor loop.

why.correct: The optic chiasm lies just above the pituitary gland. Its crossing fibers carry the outer (side) half of each eye's visual field, so a tumor pressing up on it removes side vision in both eyes.
options: Correct. Pressure on the optic chiasm removes both outer visual fields.
Growth hormone does not enlarge the eyes, and the problem here is a loss of side vision.
The occipital lobes lie far away at the back of the brain; a pituitary tumor does not reach them.
Lack of ADH causes large volumes of urine, not loss of side vision.

why.correct: Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin, released when the baby suckles, makes the cells around the milk-filled sacs contract and push milk toward the nipple. Plenty of milk that will not come out points to oxytocin.
options: Prolactin makes the milk, and she has plenty.
FSH acts on the ovaries and testes, not the breast.
TSH acts on the thyroid gland, not the breast.
Correct. Oxytocin moves milk out of the breast.

why.correct: Somatostatin, also called growth hormone–inhibiting hormone, holds back GH release. GHRH drives it.
options: Correct. Somatostatin inhibits GH release.
GHRH is the releasing hormone for GH; it raises GH.
Dopamine is the main hormone holding back prolactin.
CRH drives ACTH release, not GH.

why.correct: The ring of cells around the colloid-filled center of each follicle is made of follicular cells, which make and release T3 and T4 when TSH stimulates them.
options: Parafollicular (C) cells sit between follicles, not in the ring around the colloid.
Correct. The cells lining the follicle are the follicular cells.
Chief cells make PTH in the parathyroid glands, not in thyroid follicles.
Osteoblasts are bone-building cells, not part of the thyroid gland.

why.correct: The four small glands on the back surface of the thyroid gland are the parathyroid glands, which make PTH.
options: The thyroid gland is the larger butterfly-shaped gland; the pinned structures are the small glands on its back.
Correct. These are the parathyroid glands.
The thymus lies lower, behind the breastbone, not on the thyroid gland.
The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys, not in the neck.

why.correct: Removing the thyroid gland removes T4, T3 and calcitonin. The thyroid axis responds with a high TSH, and every tissue slows. Blood calcium stays normal because the parathyroid glands and calcitriol, not calcitonin, control it in adults.

variables.name: T4 and T3 in the blood
variables.why: The follicular cells that made them are gone; what remains is slowly cleared, and T4 has a half-life of about a week.

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: Without T4 and T3, long-loop negative feedback on the anterior pituitary is lost, so TSH rises high.

variables.name: Heat production by body cells
variables.why: Less thyroid hormone means fewer sodium–potassium pumps and mitochondria, so cells use less oxygen and make less heat.

variables.name: Calcitonin
variables.why: The parafollicular (C) cells that make calcitonin were removed with the gland.

variables.name: Blood calcium
variables.why: PTH and calcitriol, the main regulators, still work, so calcium stays normal despite losing calcitonin.

why.correct: Without iodine, the gland cannot make its hormones. Feedback is lost, TSH rises, and TSH makes the gland grow into a goiter while the person shows the slowed signs of hypothyroidism.

variables.name: T4 and T3 made by the thyroid gland
variables.why: Iodine is part of both hormones; without it the follicular cells cannot finish making them.

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: Low T4 and T3 remove long-loop negative feedback, so the anterior pituitary releases more TSH.

variables.name: Size of the thyroid gland
variables.why: High TSH keeps driving the follicular cells to grow and make thyroglobulin: a goiter.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: With less thyroid hormone, heart cells have fewer beta-1 receptor proteins and less drive, so the resting heart rate falls.

why.correct: The immune protein copies TSH but ignores feedback. Thyroid hormone rises, TSH falls, and every tissue speeds up: fast heart, weight loss, heat intolerance, and a goiter.

variables.name: T4 and T3
variables.why: The follicular cells are driven as if TSH were always present, so they release hormone nonstop.

variables.name: TSH
variables.why: High T4 and T3 feed back on the anterior pituitary and hypothalamus, suppressing TSH almost to zero.

variables.name: Resting heart rate
variables.why: More thyroid hormone means more beta-1 receptor proteins on heart cells and a stronger response to the sympathetic system.

variables.name: Body weight, with normal eating
variables.why: Cells burn more fuel and make more heat, so stores are used up despite eating.

variables.name: Size of the thyroid gland
variables.why: The immune protein drives growth just as TSH would.

why.correct: Low thyroid hormone with high TSH points to the thyroid gland itself. Her symptoms are the slowed state of hypothyroidism. With the gland failing, long-loop negative feedback is lost and the anterior pituitary pushes TSH up. In iodized-salt countries, the usual cause is Hashimoto thyroiditis.
options: A failing anterior pituitary would give a low TSH, not a high one.
Too little TRH would lower TSH, not raise it.
Overactive parathyroid glands raise blood calcium; they do not lower T4 or raise TSH.
Correct. Primary hypothyroidism: the target gland fails and TSH rises.

why.correct: If the thyroid gland had failed, TSH would be high. A low TSH with low T4 means the thyroid gland is not being driven: the anterior pituitary is making too little TSH, or the hypothalamus too little TRH.
options: A failing thyroid gland removes feedback and makes TSH rise, not fall.
The parathyroid glands control calcium, not T4 or TSH.
Correct. Too little drive from above lowers both TSH and T4.
Parafollicular cells make calcitonin, not T4, and do not control TSH.

why.correct: Without iodine the gland cannot make T4 and T3. Their fall removes long-loop negative feedback, TSH rises, and TSH makes the follicular cells multiply and make more thyroglobulin, so the gland swells into a goiter.
options: Correct. The goiter is driven by high TSH.
Iodine goes into the hormones, not into the gland's connective tissue.
Thyroglobulin stays in the colloid anyway; the swelling comes from growth driven by TSH.
Iodine has no direct shrinking action on the gland. It is used to make hormone.

why.correct: Iodide is trapped, thyroglobulin goes into the colloid, iodine is attached to its tyrosines, and pairs of iodinated tyrosines couple to form T4 and T3. The hormones stay stored in the colloid until TSH makes the cells take it back and lysosomes free them.
T4 and T3 are stored outside the cells, attached to thyroglobulin in the colloid. Parafollicular (C) cells make calcitonin, not T4 or T3.
options: This step is right. A sodium–iodide cotransporter traps iodide.
This step is right. Iodination happens on thyroglobulin at the edge of the colloid.
This is the error. The hormones are stored on thyroglobulin in the colloid, and parafollicular cells make calcitonin.
This step is right. TSH triggers endocytosis of colloid.
This step is right. Lysosomal enzymes digest thyroglobulin and free the hormones.

why.correct: The kidney step makes calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), the active form of vitamin D. PTH switches that step on.
options: Calcitonin is a peptide made by the thyroid gland's C cells, not a form of vitamin D.
PTH switches on the kidney step but is made by the parathyroid glands.
Thyroxine is a thyroid hormone, made from tyrosine and iodine.
Correct. The kidneys make calcitriol.

why.correct: PTH raises blood calcium: it drives bone breakdown by osteoclasts (acting through osteoblasts), makes the kidneys keep calcium and lose phosphate, and switches on calcitriol production.
options: Correct. PTH drives osteoclast activity.
Correct. PTH makes the kidneys pull calcium back from the urine.
PTH does the opposite: it makes the kidneys lose phosphate in the urine.
Correct. PTH switches on the kidney enzyme that makes calcitriol.
Switching osteoclasts off is calcitonin's action, not PTH's.

why.correct: PTH binds receptor proteins on osteoblasts. The osteoblasts then release a signal that makes more osteoclasts form and makes existing ones more active. Osteocytes, which develop from osteoblasts, carry the same receptor protein and send the same signal. Osteoclasts themselves have no PTH receptor protein.
options: C cells are in the thyroid gland, not bone, and they make calcitonin.
Osteoclasts respond to PTH only indirectly, through the osteoblasts' signal.
Chondrocytes are cartilage cells and are not the relay for PTH's effect on bone breakdown.
Correct. Osteoblasts receive PTH and signal the osteoclasts.

why.correct: The parathyroid glands sit on the back of the thyroid gland and are easily injured in thyroid surgery. Without PTH, blood calcium falls. Low extracellular calcium makes voltage-gated sodium channels open more easily, so nerves and muscles fire on their own: tingling, cramps and tetany.
options: Losing calcitonin would, if anything, let calcium rise, and high calcium makes nerves less excitable, not more.
T4 has a half-life of about a week, so it cannot have fallen enough in one day, and lack of it slows reflexes rather than causing cramps.
Correct. Hypoparathyroidism after surgery causes hypocalcemia and tetany.
TSH acts on the thyroid gland, not on muscles, and it would not cause tetany.

why.correct: Too much PTH releases calcium from bone (bone pain), keeps calcium in the blood and drives phosphate into the urine. High calcium and low phosphate with a high PTH is hyperparathyroidism, usually from a benign tumor of one gland. Extra calcium in the urine forms stones.
options: Hypoparathyroidism gives low PTH and low calcium, the opposite pattern.
Vitamin D deficiency raises PTH, but blood calcium is low or low-normal, not high.
Correct. High PTH with high calcium and low phosphate is hyperparathyroidism.
Hypothyroidism causes tiredness but does not raise calcium and PTH or cause stones.

why.correct: In adults, PTH and calcitriol are the main regulators of blood calcium. When calcium rises, PTH release falls, so less calcium comes from bone, the kidneys and the gut. People with no thyroid gland keep normal calcium as long as their parathyroid glands work.
options: Correct. Calcitonin's role in adults is small.
Calcium does not climb without calcitonin: falling PTH is the main brake when calcium rises.
Calcitonin lowers calcium; losing it could not make calcium very low.
The PTH loop keeps calcium steady from day to day without calcitonin.

why.correct: Calcitonin comes from the parafollicular (C) cells, which sit between the follicles of the thyroid gland.
options: Follicular cells make T4 and T3.
Chief cells make parathyroid hormone.
Correct. C cells make calcitonin.
Osteoclasts are a target of calcitonin, not its source.

why.correct: Too little vitamin D leaves too little calcitriol, so too little calcium and phosphate are absorbed to mineralize new matrix. In an adult, whose epiphyseal plates have closed, this soft bone is osteomalacia.
options: Rickets is the same problem in children, affecting their growing bones and epiphyseal plates.
In osteoporosis there is too little bone, but what remains is normally mineralized.
Correct. Soft, poorly mineralized bone in an adult is osteomalacia.
Her PTH is probably raised as a response, but the root problem is the lack of vitamin D, which is what leaves her matrix poorly mineralized.

why.correct: Low vitamin D means low calcitriol and poor calcium absorption. PTH rises to defend blood calcium, taking calcium from bone and dumping phosphate. Too little calcium phosphate reaches new bone matrix, causing rickets or osteomalacia.

variables.name: Calcitriol
variables.why: Less vitamin D reaches the liver and kidneys to be activated.

variables.name: Calcium absorbed by the intestine
variables.why: Without calcitriol, the intestinal cells make fewer of the proteins that absorb calcium.

variables.name: PTH
variables.why: The small dip in blood calcium makes the chief cells release more PTH.

variables.name: Phosphate lost in the urine
variables.why: The higher PTH makes the kidneys keep less phosphate.

why.correct: Thyroid hormone is essential for brain growth and myelination after birth. Affected babies often look normal for weeks, partly from their mother's hormone. By the time signs appear, some damage is permanent; T4 tablets started in the first two weeks prevent it.
options: Correct. No early signs, and the harm cannot be undone later.
Screening measures the baby's own thyroid function, not the mother's iodine intake.
Thyroid hormone is needed throughout life, especially for the first two to three years of brain growth.
Goiter in adults has other causes, such as iodine deficiency and Graves disease.

why.correct: Panel 3b shows kidney tubule cells moving calcium from the urine side into the blood, and releasing calcitriol into the blood. Both raise blood calcium.
options: The figure shows calcium moving out of the urine, not into it, and calcitonin comes from the thyroid gland, not the kidneys.
Absorbing calcium from food is done by intestinal cells, driven by calcitriol, in panel 3c.
Building bone from blood calcium is shown in the calcitonin panel, not the kidney panel.
Correct. PTH makes the kidneys keep calcium and make calcitriol.

why.correct: Step 4 shows the arrows from T3 and T4 returning with a minus sign: elevated T3 and T4 inhibit TRH and TSH release. This is long-loop negative feedback.
options: Correct. The thyroid hormones feed back on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
TSH is driven by TRH; a rise in TSH does not stop TRH in this figure.
Calcitonin plays no part in the thyroid axis.
The figure shows thyroid hormones raising body temperature; a fall in temperature is not what stops TRH here.

why.correct: Most T3 in your body is made outside the thyroid gland: enzymes in the liver, kidneys and target cells snip one iodine off T4. T4 is a long-lasting reserve that tissues activate as needed.
options: The tablet does not pass through the thyroid gland; it is absorbed into the blood from the gut.
TSH acts on the thyroid gland; it does not bind or activate T4.
Correct. Tissues remove one iodine from T4 to make T3.
T4 is absorbed intact; conversion happens in tissues, not in the stomach.

why.correct: The kidneys carry out the final step in making calcitriol. Diseased kidneys make too little, so the intestine absorbs little calcium. Blood calcium falls, and the healthy parathyroid glands respond by releasing more and more PTH.
options: Correct. Low calcitriol means poor calcium absorption, and PTH rises in response.
The kidneys do not make calcitonin; the thyroid gland's C cells do.
The thyroid axis does not set blood calcium.
Calcitonin lowers calcium; losing a response to it would not make calcium low.

why.correct: Too much thyroid hormone speeds every tissue: more heat (warm, moist skin), more fuel burned (weight loss), more sympathetic sensitivity (fast heart, tremor). In Graves disease TSH is suppressed by feedback, not high.
options: Correct. More beta-1 receptor proteins and sympathetic sensitivity speed the heart.
Feeling cold is a sign of too little thyroid hormone. Hyperthyroid people feel hot.
Correct. Cells burn fuel faster than it is eaten.
Correct. Greater sympathetic sensitivity causes a fine tremor.
In Graves disease the high T4 and T3 suppress TSH almost to zero.
Correct. Extra heat production makes the skin warm and sweaty.

why.correct: Thyroid hormones are lipid-soluble: T3 binds a receptor protein in the nucleus and changes transcription, so new proteins take time to build up. T4's half-life of about a week also means its blood level keeps climbing for about five to six weeks before it levels off, which is why TSH is rechecked after about six weeks.
options: Thyroid hormones act through a receptor protein in the nucleus, not in the membrane.
T4 is converted to T3, not TSH. TSH is a pituitary hormone.
The pituitary does not need to shrink; TSH simply falls as feedback returns.
Correct. Gene-level action and a long half-life make the effect slow.

why.correct: Alpha cells, about a third of the cells in a human islet, release glucagon when blood glucose falls.
options: Beta cells release insulin, the hormone that lowers blood glucose.
Delta cells release somatostatin, a local signal that holds back both insulin and glucagon.
Correct. Alpha cells make glucagon.
PP cells release pancreatic polypeptide, which slows the pancreas's digestive secretions.

why.correct: The beta cell is its own glucose sensor. More glucose inside means more ATP. ATP shuts potassium channels, so less positive charge leaks out and the membrane depolarizes. That opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and the incoming calcium triggers exocytosis of insulin.

Insulin release depends on ATP closing these channels. With them held open, potassium keeps leaking out, the membrane cannot depolarize, voltage-gated calcium channels stay closed, and without calcium entry the insulin vesicles are not released.
options: Correct. With the channels held open, potassium keeps leaking out, the membrane cannot depolarize, voltage-gated calcium channels stay closed, and without calcium entry the insulin vesicles are not released.
Open potassium channels let potassium flow out, down its gradient, not in. Outward flow keeps the inside negative, which works against depolarization.
The drug acts on the potassium channel, not on glucose entry. Glucose still enters and raises ATP; the step after ATP is blocked.
Depolarization needs the potassium channels to close. Holding them open does the opposite.

why.correct: Insulin moves GLUT4 into muscle and fat cell membranes, drives glycogen building, stops the liver making and releasing glucose, stores fat, and moves potassium into cells.
options: Correct. This is how insulin lets glucose into muscle and fat.
Glycogenolysis releases glucose from storage, which is glucagon's action. Insulin switches it off.
Correct. Insulin drives glucose into glycogen in the liver and muscle.
Insulin does the reverse: it builds triglycerides and blocks their breakdown.
Correct. Insulin speeds the sodium–potassium pump, which is why it is used to lower a high blood potassium.
Correct. Insulin stops the liver making new glucose.

why.correct: Glucagon, the fasting signal, acts on the liver because muscle has almost no receptor proteins for it. And even when a muscle cell breaks down its glycogen, it lacks the enzyme that frees glucose to leave the cell, so that glucose fuels only the muscle itself.
options: Insulin promotes building glycogen, not releasing it. Muscle glycogen is broken down during exercise, when insulin is low.
A resting muscle uses little fuel overnight, and much of what it burns is fat. Its glycogen stores are largely intact in the morning.
Correct. No glucagon signal reaches muscle, and a muscle cell lacks the enzyme that frees glucose to leave it.
Muscle does not turn its glycogen into fat. It keeps the glycogen to fuel its own contractions.

why.correct: Insulin rises within minutes of the meal and peaks with glucose. It moves GLUT4 into muscle and fat membranes and makes the liver store glucose as glycogen, so glucose leaves the blood. As glucose falls, insulin falls too: negative feedback.
options: Glucagon falls after a carbohydrate meal, and it would raise blood glucose, not lower it.
Correct. The insulin curve rises and falls with the glucose curve.
Glucose appears in the urine only above about 180 mg/dL. This person peaks near 135, so the kidneys return all of it.
The brain uses glucose at a steady rate of about 5 grams an hour. That alone cannot clear a meal's 50 grams or more in two hours.

why.correct: Before a meal, blood glucose comes mainly from the liver. In type 2 diabetes the liver is insulin resistant, so it keeps running glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis through the night, and fasting glucose starts near 140 instead of below 100.
options: A meal is absorbed within a few hours. After an overnight fast, blood glucose reflects what the liver releases, not the last meal.
Reabsorbing too little glucose would lose glucose to the urine and lower blood glucose, not raise it.
Type 2 diabetes does not destroy islet cells, and losing alpha cells would lower glucose, not raise it.
Correct. An insulin-resistant liver overproduces glucose while fasting.

why.correct: 50 mg/dL is hypoglycemia. Alpha cells release glucagon, which switches on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver, and glucose flows back into the blood.
options: Insulin lowers blood glucose. That is the response to a high reading such as 160 mg/dL.
Alpha cells make glucagon, not insulin, and taking up more glucose would lower the reading further.
Beta cells make insulin, and stopping gluconeogenesis would lower glucose, not raise it.
Correct. Glucagon raises glucose by switching on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver.

why.correct: Losing insulin raises glucose; losing the beta cells' brake raises glucagon too. Glucose spills into the urine and drags water with it, shrinking blood volume and driving thirst. Fat breakdown runs unchecked, the liver turns the fatty acids into acids that build up in the blood, and breathing deepens to blow off carbon dioxide. Untreated, this becomes a life-threatening emergency.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: With no insulin, muscle and fat take up little glucose and the liver keeps releasing it.

variables.name: Plasma glucagon
variables.why: Insulin from neighboring beta cells normally damps the alpha cells. With the beta cells gone, that brake is lost.

variables.name: Glucose in the urine
variables.why: Blood glucose is above the roughly 180 mg/dL the kidney's carriers can fully reabsorb, so the excess stays in the urine.

variables.name: Urine volume
variables.why: Glucose left in the kidney's fluid holds water there by osmosis: polyuria.

variables.name: Blood volume
variables.why: Water lost in the extra urine comes from the plasma.

variables.name: Body weight
variables.why: Calories leave as urine glucose, and with no insulin, fat and muscle are broken down.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: Unchecked fat breakdown and high glucagon make the liver turn fatty acids into acids faster than tissues can burn them.

variables.name: Depth and rate of breathing
variables.why: Acid in the blood drives faster, deeper breathing, which blows off carbon dioxide and partly offsets the acid.

why.correct: Injected insulin lowers glucose by moving it into muscle and fat and by shutting down liver output. It also moves potassium into cells. The falling glucose then triggers glucagon release, the first step of the body's defense against hypoglycemia.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Insulin drives glucose into muscle and fat and stops the liver releasing it.

variables.name: GLUT4 carriers in the membrane of muscle cells
variables.why: Insulin moves GLUT4 from vesicles inside the cell to the plasma membrane.

variables.name: Glucose output from the liver
variables.why: Insulin switches off glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

variables.name: Plasma glucagon
variables.why: Falling glucose stimulates the alpha cells, the counterregulatory response.

variables.name: Plasma potassium
variables.why: Insulin speeds the sodium–potassium pump, moving potassium into cells.

why.correct: He is unconscious from hypoglycemia, so nothing may go into his mouth: he could choke. Glucagon switches on glycogenolysis in his liver, releasing glucose into his blood within minutes.
options: Correct. He is unconscious, so nothing may go into his mouth. Glucagon switches on glycogenolysis in his liver and raises his glucose within minutes.
Fast sugar by mouth is right for a conscious person, but an unresponsive person cannot swallow safely and could choke.
Insulin would drive his glucose lower still. The problem is too much insulin action, not too little.
His brain is starved of glucose now. His own defenses have already failed to hold his glucose up against the injected insulin, and he could seize or suffer brain injury.

why.correct: The brain runs almost entirely on glucose from the blood, minute by minute. Muscle can burn fatty acids and its own glycogen, so it keeps working when blood glucose falls.
options: Neurons take up glucose through carriers that are always in their membranes, with no need for insulin.
The sympathetic response causes shakiness, sweating and a fast heart. It does not shut down the brain; the lack of glucose does.
Gluconeogenesis happens in the liver and, in a long fast, the kidneys. Muscle cannot release glucose into the blood.
Correct. The brain has no fuel reserve and no fallback fuel for sudden lows, so it depends on glucose from the blood minute by minute.

why.correct: Untreated type 1 diabetes has left her with almost no insulin. With nothing to hold back fat breakdown, and glucagon high, her liver turns fatty acids into acidic fuel molecules faster than her tissues can burn them, and they build up in her blood. One of them is breathed out and gives the fruity smell.
options: Her breathing muscles are not working hard enough to acidify her blood, and lactic acid does not explain the fruity breath.
Correct. With no insulin, fat breakdown runs unchecked and the liver turns the fatty acids into acids that build up in the blood.
Glucose is not an acid in the body. Its high level causes the polyuria and dehydration, not the acid.
Her deep, fast breathing is blowing carbon dioxide off, which partly offsets the acid. It is a response, not the cause.

why.correct: Above about 180 mg/dL, the kidney's carriers cannot take back all the filtered glucose. The glucose left behind holds water by osmosis, so more water leaves as urine. The thirst comes after, from the water lost.
options: Correct. The glucose drags water with it: polyuria.
High glucose raises plasma concentration, which increases ADH release, not decreases it.
Insulin does not control water handling by the kidneys. Its absence acts through the high glucose.
That gets the order backwards. The water loss comes first and causes the thirst.

why.correct: High glucose together with high insulin means her tissues respond too little to insulin: insulin resistance. Her beta cells are releasing extra insulin but can no longer keep glucose normal. That is type 2 diabetes. A fasting glucose of 126 or above, confirmed on a second test, meets the diagnostic cutoff.
options: In type 1 diabetes the beta cells are destroyed and insulin is very low or absent, not high.
Her glucose is high, not low. The high insulin is failing to lower it.
Correct. High glucose despite high insulin is the signature of insulin resistance.
A fasting glucose of 138 mg/dL is well above the normal range of 70 to 99.

why.correct: mg/dL = mmol/L × 18 = 5.0 × 18 = 90 mg/dL, inside the normal fasting range.
options: 23 comes from adding 18 to 5.0. The conversion multiplies.
0.28 comes from dividing 5.0 by 18, which converts the wrong way.
180 is 10 × 18. The reading is 5.0 mmol/L, not 10.

why.correct: Skeletal muscle has almost no glucagon receptor proteins and lacks the enzyme that lets glucose leave the cell. Between meals, blood glucose comes from the liver.
options: This step is right. Tissues keep using glucose between meals, so it drifts down.
This step is right. Low glucose stimulates alpha cells and quiets beta cells.
This step is right. Glucagon acts through a G protein–coupled receptor protein and cyclic AMP.
This step is right. The liver releases stored glucose and makes new glucose.
This is the error. Muscle glycogen stays in the muscle; only the liver releases glucose into the blood.

why.correct: Gluconeogenesis: gluc/o = glucose, neo- = new, -genesis = making. The liver does most of it.
options: Glycolysis is the breakdown of glucose in cellular respiration, the opposite direction.
Correct. New glucose from molecules that are not carbohydrates.
Glycogenesis is building glycogen, the first term in the list.
Cellular respiration breaks fuel down to make ATP. It uses glucose rather than making it.

why.correct: Muscle contraction moves GLUT4 carriers into the plasma membrane through its own pathway, which does not depend on insulin. Working muscle takes up glucose even when it resists insulin's signal.
options: Exercise lowers insulin release, through sympathetic activity on the beta cells. The glucose uptake does not come from more insulin.
Glucagon raises blood glucose. It does rise during long exercise, but it cannot explain a smaller rise.
Glucose reaches the urine only above about 180 mg/dL, and walking does not increase it.
Correct. Exercise opens a second, insulin-independent route for glucose into muscle.

why.correct: Low glucose, amino acids and sympathetic signals all raise glucagon release. Insulin and somatostatin inside the islet hold it back.
options: Correct. Low glucose is the main stimulus.
Correct. Amino acids raise both insulin and glucagon, so a protein meal does not drop your glucose.
Insulin from beta cells damps the alpha cells next door. Losing that brake is why glucagon is high in type 1 diabetes.
Correct. Epinephrine and sympathetic nerves raise glucagon, as in exercise or fear.
Somatostatin holds back the release of both insulin and glucagon.

why.correct: The pancreas lies behind the stomach, across the back of the upper abdomen. Most of it releases digestive enzymes into ducts; its scattered pancreatic islets release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
options: The adrenal glands are the small caps on the kidneys, drawn just below the pinned organ in this figure.
Correct. The long organ drawn across the upper abdomen, above the kidneys, is the pancreas.
The kidneys are the small bean-shaped organs drawn below the pinned organ.
The spleen sits high on the left side of the abdomen, beside the stomach, and is not drawn on this endocrine view.

why.correct: Blocking fat breakdown takes much less insulin than moving glucose into cells. People with type 2 diabetes still make insulin, often a lot, so their fat stores stay mostly locked and little fat reaches the liver to be turned into acids. In type 1, with almost no insulin, fat breakdown runs unchecked.
options: Correct. Some insulin keeps fat breakdown, and so the acid production, in check.
Glucose can be very high in type 2 diabetes. The acid blood depends on insulin lack, not on the glucose level.
Anyone's liver can make these acids; yours makes some during a long fast. The difference is how much fat reaches the liver.
Glucagon is present, and often high, in type 2 diabetes.

why.correct: The adrenal glands sit like caps on the upper end of each kidney (ad- = near, ren- = kidney). Each has an outer cortex that makes steroids and an inner medulla that makes epinephrine.
options: Correct. The adrenal glands cap the kidneys.
The kidneys are the larger bean-shaped organs the pinned glands sit on.
The pancreas is the long organ drawn across the abdomen above the pinned glands.
The thyroid gland is in the neck, well above the pinned structures.

why.correct: The zona fasciculata (fascicul- = little bundle) is the thickest layer of the cortex. Its cells line up in columns, and it makes cortisol, the main glucocorticoid.
options: The zona glomerulosa is the thin outer layer of rounded clusters (glomerul- = little ball). It makes aldosterone.
The zona reticularis is the inner layer of branching cords (reticul- = little net). It makes androgens such as DHEA.
The medulla is the core, with larger round chromaffin cells, not columns. It makes epinephrine.
Correct. Columns of cells in the thickest layer: the zona fasciculata, making cortisol.

why.correct: Low pressure in the kidney triggers renin release. Renin makes angiotensin I from angiotensinogen; ACE makes angiotensin II; angiotensin II releases aldosterone; aldosterone makes the kidney keep sodium, and water follows by osmosis, restoring volume.
Angiotensinogen is a protein in the plasma, made and released by the liver, all the time. The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.
options: This step is right. Low pressure in the kidney's small arteries is a main trigger for renin.
This is the error. The liver, not the adrenal medulla, makes angiotensinogen.
This step is right. Renin is an enzyme that cuts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
This step is right. ACE, most plentiful in the lungs, makes the active hormone.
This step is right. Angiotensin II acts on the zona glomerulosa of the cortex.

why.correct: Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is the tropic hormone of the adrenal axis: CRH → ACTH → cortisol.
options: TSH drives the thyroid gland, in the thyroid axis (TRH → TSH → thyroid hormones).
ADH is released from the posterior pituitary and acts on the kidney's water handling, not on the adrenal cortex.
Correct. ACTH drives the zona fasciculata.
Renin comes from the kidney and starts the angiotensin chain that controls aldosterone, not cortisol.

why.correct: During treatment, feedback from the drug suppresses ACTH and the zona fasciculata shrinks. When the drug stops suddenly, glucocorticoid activity crashes: blood glucose and blood pressure fall, the picture of an adrenal crisis. ACTH stays low at first, and it rises only over weeks to months, while the shrunken cortex recovers more slowly still. That is why long courses of glucocorticoids are tapered.

variables.name: ACTH, during treatment
variables.why: The drug acts like cortisol on the hypothalamus and pituitary, so long-loop feedback suppresses CRH and ACTH.

variables.name: Size of his zona fasciculata, during treatment
variables.why: ACTH keeps the zona fasciculata large; without it, the layer shrinks over weeks.

variables.name: His own cortisol release, during treatment
variables.why: With little ACTH, the shrunken zona fasciculata makes little cortisol.

variables.name: Total glucocorticoid activity, in the days after stopping
variables.why: The drug is gone, and his shrunken adrenal cortex cannot make up for it quickly.

variables.name: Blood glucose, in the days after stopping
variables.why: Without glucocorticoid, the liver makes less glucose by gluconeogenesis.

variables.name: Blood pressure, in the days after stopping
variables.why: Cortisol is permissive for the vessels' response to norepinephrine and epinephrine; without it, vessels constrict poorly.

variables.name: ACTH, in the days after stopping
variables.why: The hypothalamus and pituitary were suppressed for months and take weeks to restart, so ACTH stays low at first; that is why the crisis comes on so fast.

why.correct: This is Cushing disease. Excess ACTH raises cortisol and adrenal androgens and enlarges both cortices, while feedback from the high cortisol shuts down CRH. Aldosterone is largely unaffected, because its main drivers are angiotensin II and potassium.

variables.name: Plasma cortisol
variables.why: ACTH drives the zona fasciculata to make cortisol.

variables.name: CRH release from the hypothalamus
variables.why: High cortisol feeds back on the hypothalamus. The tumor ignores the feedback, but the hypothalamus still obeys it.

variables.name: Size of both adrenal cortices
variables.why: Constant ACTH makes the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis grow.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Cortisol raises gluconeogenesis and makes muscle and fat resist insulin.

variables.name: Adrenal androgens
variables.why: ACTH also drives the zona reticularis, which makes DHEA.

variables.name: Aldosterone
variables.why: Aldosterone is driven mainly by angiotensin II and potassium; ACTH has only a small, short-lived effect on it.

why.correct: This is Addison disease, primary adrenal insufficiency. Low cortisol explains the weakness, weight loss and low glucose; low aldosterone explains the salt loss, high potassium and faintness. Feedback no longer holds back the pituitary, so ACTH rises very high, and high ACTH darkens the skin.
options: Her ACTH is very high, not low. Pituitary failure would also spare aldosterone and would not darken her skin.
Correct. Both cortisol and aldosterone are low, and ACTH is high, so the cortex itself has failed.
Losing epinephrine alone causes little, because sympathetic nerves cover its effects. It cannot explain the high potassium or dark skin.
Too much CRH would raise ACTH and so raise cortisol, giving high glucose, not low.

why.correct: Her Cushing syndrome comes from the drug, the most common cause. Prednisone acts like cortisol on the hypothalamus and pituitary, and long-loop feedback suppresses CRH and ACTH. Her own adrenal cortex shrinks.
options: Correct. The drug suppresses ACTH through negative feedback.
High ACTH causes Cushing syndrome when a tumor releases it. Here the glucocorticoid comes from outside, and feedback suppresses ACTH.
A large dose of glucocorticoid for a year does not leave the axis unchanged: feedback turns ACTH down.
Her adrenal glands shrink because ACTH is low, not the other way round. The drug's feedback holds ACTH down.

why.correct: Blocking ACE lowers angiotensin II, so the zona glomerulosa releases less aldosterone. With less aldosterone, the kidney secretes less potassium into the urine, and plasma potassium rises. Clinicians check potassium after starting these drugs.
options: Correct. Blocking ACE lowers angiotensin II, so the zona glomerulosa releases less aldosterone. With less aldosterone, the kidney secretes less potassium into the urine, and plasma potassium rises. Clinicians check potassium after starting these drugs.
Potassium excretion falls, not rises, when aldosterone falls, so plasma potassium cannot fall for this reason.
Aldosterone is a main control of potassium excretion, so lowering it changes potassium.

why.correct: High potassium acts directly on zona glomerulosa cells, which release aldosterone. Aldosterone makes the last stretch of the kidney's tubes secrete more potassium into the urine, and plasma potassium falls: negative feedback.
options: Cortisol's main effects are on fuel, inflammation and blood vessels. Handling potassium is aldosterone's job.
Epinephrine does shift potassium into cells briefly, but the adrenal cortex's response to high potassium is aldosterone.
Correct. High potassium is a direct stimulus for aldosterone.
DHEA is a weak androgen with no role in handling potassium.

why.correct: Cortisol raises blood glucose by driving gluconeogenesis, breaking down muscle protein for its amino acids and making tissues resist insulin. It is permissive for the vessels' response to sympathetic signals. It damps inflammation and slows bone building.
options: Correct. Cortisol switches on gluconeogenesis.
Correct. The amino acids feed gluconeogenesis; in excess, muscles waste.
Cortisol damps inflammation, which is why glucocorticoid drugs treat inflammatory diseases.
Correct. This permissive effect is why low cortisol causes low blood pressure.
Cortisol slows bone building; long-term excess thins bone.
Correct. Muscle and fat take up less glucose, which leaves more in the blood; in excess this causes high blood glucose.

why.correct: In pituitary failure, ACTH is low, so nothing darkens the skin. Cortisol falls, but the zona glomerulosa still answers angiotensin II and potassium, so aldosterone is mostly spared and potassium stays normal. In Addison disease the cortex itself is destroyed, so aldosterone falls too, and very high ACTH darkens the skin.
options: The pituitary does not make aldosterone; only the zona glomerulosa does.
Correct. Low ACTH means no darkening, and aldosterone keeps its own controls.
The medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. It cannot make steroids.
Nothing changes the tissues' responses. The difference lies in which hormones are low.

why.correct: Much of the medulla's blood arrives from the cortex, rich in cortisol. Cortisol keeps up the enzyme that converts norepinephrine into epinephrine, so with little cortisol the medulla makes less epinephrine.
options: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptor proteins of the chromaffin cells.
Chromaffin cells develop from the same embryonic tissue as postganglionic sympathetic neurons, not from cortex cells.
Epinephrine is an amine made from the amino acid tyrosine; cortisol is a steroid. One is not made from the other.
Correct. The shared blood supply lets the cortex set how much epinephrine the medulla can make.

why.correct: With liver glycogen gone, glucose must be made new. Cortisol, with glucagon, switches on gluconeogenesis in the liver and breaks down muscle protein to supply amino acids for it.
options: Correct. Cortisol drives gluconeogenesis from amino acids.
Aldosterone controls sodium and potassium. Sodium is not a fuel.
Epinephrine releases glucose from liver glycogen, but the glycogen is gone after the first day.
Insulin lowers blood glucose and is low during fasting.

why.correct: The alarm reaction is the fight-or-flight response, acting in seconds through sympathetic nerves and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla. Epinephrine speeds the heart and switches on glycogenolysis in the liver.
options: Cortisol acts over hours through new proteins. It carries the stage of resistance, not the first seconds.
Correct. The seconds-long response is sympathetic and epinephrine-driven.
Aldosterone takes hours to act and handles sodium and potassium, not heart rate.
The stage of exhaustion comes after weeks or months of unrelieved stress.

why.correct: Cortisol can bind aldosterone's receptor protein and circulates at far higher levels. Normally an enzyme in the kidney's aldosterone-sensitive cells inactivates it. With the enzyme blocked, cortisol acts like aldosterone: sodium and water are kept, potassium is lost, pressure rises, and the higher volume turns renin and aldosterone down.
options: Licorice contains no aldosterone; its effect comes from letting the body's own cortisol act on the kidney.
Epinephrine could raise pressure but would not explain the low potassium with low renin and aldosterone.
If the kidney stopped responding to aldosterone, he would lose sodium and keep potassium, the opposite of his findings.
Correct. Unprotected cortisol mimics aldosterone.

why.correct: Cortex hormones are steroids built from cholesterol. They cross the plasma membrane, bind an intracellular receptor protein, and switch genes on or off. Building new proteins takes hours, and the effects last.
options: Steroids are not stored in vesicles; they diffuse out as soon as they are made.
Hormones travel in the blood, not along nerves.
Correct. Changing gene expression is slow to start and slow to wear off.
Steroids act as they are. Epinephrine is a different kind of hormone, an amine made in the medulla.

why.correct: In women, the adrenal glands are a main source of androgen. DHEA is weak itself, but tissues convert it into stronger androgens, which support pubic and underarm hair and contribute to sex drive. In adult men, the testes make far more.
options: Sodium is set by aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa.
The monthly release of an egg is triggered by the pituitary's gonadotropins, not by adrenal androgens.
Cortisol, from the zona fasciculata, raises blood glucose during fasting.
Correct. Adrenal androgens matter most in women.

why.correct: Under ordinary chronic stress, the axis keeps working: cortisol is usually normal or high, or its daily rhythm flattens. The harm of the stage of exhaustion comes from prolonged exposure, some of the same effects as cortisol excess. "Adrenal fatigue" is not a recognized diagnosis. Exams may still expect "resources are depleted".
options: Cortisol does not vanish under chronic stress. A truly failed cortex is Addison disease, a separate illness.
Correct. The glands do not wear out; long exposure does the damage.
The medulla keeps working under chronic stress; nothing shows it shrinking.
Aldosterone handles sodium and potassium. It does not take over cortisol's role.

why.correct: The thymus sits in the mediastinum, behind the upper sternum and in front of the heart. It is largest in childhood, when white blood cells mature there under the influence of its thymosins.
options: The thyroid gland is in the neck, wrapped around the front of the trachea, above the pinned organ.
Correct. The thymus lies in the upper chest, behind the sternum.
The trachea is the airway running down the neck into the chest, not the gland in front of the heart.
Lymph nodes are small, bean-shaped structures found in clusters, especially in the neck, armpits and groin.

why.correct: The ovaries sit in the pelvis, one on each side. Besides releasing eggs, they are endocrine glands that make estrogens and progesterone.
options: The adrenal glands cap the kidneys, high in the abdomen.
The kidneys lie high on the back wall of the abdomen, well above the pelvis.
Correct. The paired glands in the female pelvis are the ovaries.
The pancreas lies across the upper abdomen, behind the stomach.

why.correct: Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells report light to the suprachiasmatic nucleus. At night their signal stops, and the SCN's output lets a sympathetic pathway, relayed through the spinal cord and the superior cervical ganglion, release norepinephrine onto pinealocytes. They convert serotonin to melatonin and release it.

Light, especially blue-rich light, excites melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells, which signal the suprachiasmatic nucleus. The sympathetic drive to the pineal gland is shut off, so melatonin release falls. Evening light also shifts the body clock later.
options: Visual effort does not drive the pineal gland. Light suppresses melatonin, whatever the eyes are looking at.
Correct. Light at the retina switches off melatonin release.
Artificial light works through the same retinal cells as sunlight, though bright light has more effect than dim light.
In humans, the pineal gland does not sense light itself. The signal comes from the retina through the SCN and a sympathetic pathway, and light lowers melatonin rather than raising it.

why.correct: Light is the strongest signal for resetting the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Morning light moves the clock earlier, which is what an eastward flight requires. A small dose of melatonin in the evening at the new bedtime also helps.
options: Correct. Morning light pulls the clock earlier.
Darkness removes the main resetting signal, so the clock would stay on New York time longer.
Melatonin taken in the morning signals "night" at the wrong time and tends to shift the clock the wrong way.
Meal timing has a small effect on clocks in the body's organs, but it does not reset the master clock as strongly as light.

why.correct: The suprachiasmatic nucleus, a pair of tiny clusters of neurons just above the optic chiasm, keeps time through a loop of clock genes and keeps the clocks in other cells in step.
options: The pineal gland releases melatonin on the SCN's instructions. It is an output of the clock, not the clock itself.
The anterior pituitary's hormones follow daily rhythms set by the clock, but it does not keep time itself.
The retina sends light information to the clock to reset it; it does not keep time for the body.
Correct. The SCN is the master clock.

why.correct: Stretched muscle cells in the heart's upper chambers release atrial natriuretic peptide. ANP makes the kidneys filter more and reabsorb less sodium, lowers renin, aldosterone and ADH, and dilates vessels, so the extra volume is excreted: negative feedback.
options: ANP lowers aldosterone. Aldosterone would keep more sodium, raising volume further.
Stretch raises ANP release, not lowers it.
Correct. Stretch releases ANP, which lowers blood volume.
Higher volume and ANP both lower renin release.

why.correct: At altitude the arterial blood carries less oxygen, and the kidneys respond within hours by releasing EPO. Red blood cells rise only over weeks. Once they have, the blood carries more oxygen, the kidney's oxygen supply improves, and EPO falls back.

variables.name: Oxygen in her arterial blood, first day
variables.why: Each breath carries less oxygen at lower air pressure, so she is hypoxemic.

variables.name: EPO release from her kidneys, first day
variables.why: Kidney cells sense less oxygen, and the oxygen-sensing protein survives and switches on the EPO gene within hours.

variables.name: Red blood cell count, first day
variables.why: EPO acts on the bone marrow, and new red blood cells take days to weeks to appear in large numbers.

variables.name: Red blood cell count, after six weeks
variables.why: Weeks of raised EPO have increased red blood cell production.

variables.name: Oxygen carried per liter of her blood, after six weeks
variables.why: More red blood cells in each liter carry more oxygen, partly offsetting the thin air.

variables.name: EPO release, after six weeks compared with the first day
variables.why: The extra red blood cells deliver more oxygen to the kidney, so EPO release eases back toward normal: negative feedback.

why.correct: After a large bleed, the blood that remains is normally loaded with oxygen, so there is no hypoxemia. But there are too few red blood cells and too little flow, so the tissues receive too little oxygen: hypoxia.
options: At altitude, each breath brings in less oxygen, so the arterial blood itself is low in oxygen: hypoxemia, with hypoxia.
Lung disease impairs loading oxygen into the blood, so the arterial blood is low in oxygen: hypoxemia.
Breathing too slowly brings too little fresh air into the lungs, so arterial oxygen falls: hypoxemia.
Correct. The blood is fully loaded but there is not enough of it reaching the tissues.

why.correct: The oxygen-sensing cells of the kidney make erythropoietin. When kidney tissue is lost, EPO falls, the bone marrow gets too little signal to make red blood cells, and the count falls. Injections of synthetic EPO correct it.
options: Long-term kidney disease does not usually leak whole red blood cells into the urine in large numbers.
Correct. Too little EPO means too little red blood cell production.
Nothing suggests his bone marrow is replaced; it lacks the hormone signal, not the capacity.
ANP comes from the heart and acts on sodium and water; it does not control red blood cell production.

why.correct: Leptin rises in proportion to fat stores, but in most obesity the hypothalamus responds weakly to it: leptin resistance. That is why giving more leptin helps only the rare people born unable to make it.
options: Correct. This is leptin resistance.
The leptin is normal and active; the weak link is the brain's response to it.
Leptin acts in adults too: adults born without it stay severely hungry until they are treated with it.
High leptin signals that energy stores are full and normally lowers food intake. It does not reverse its own effect.

why.correct: Leptin tracks fat stores. With very little fat, leptin is low, and the hypothalamus turns down GnRH. Less GnRH means less FSH and LH, the ovaries make less estrogen, and periods stop.
options: Her leptin is low, not high, because leptin rises with fat stores.
Melatonin is a timing signal from the pineal gland; it does not explain periods stopping with low body fat.
EPO controls red blood cell production and is not the link between body fat and periods.
Correct. Low leptin tells the reproductive axis that energy stores are too small.

why.correct: The drug builds muscle, but it also switches off his own reproductive axis by negative feedback. LH and FSH fall, so his testes shrink and make less testosterone and fewer sperm. After he stops, recovery can take months.

variables.name: LH and FSH from his anterior pituitary
variables.why: High androgen feeds back on the hypothalamus and pituitary, cutting GnRH, LH and FSH.

variables.name: Testosterone made by his own testes
variables.why: Without LH, his testes make little testosterone of their own.

variables.name: Size of his testes
variables.why: Without LH and FSH, the testes are no longer driven and shrink.

variables.name: Sperm production
variables.why: Sperm production needs FSH and a high testosterone level inside the testes, both of which fall.

variables.name: Skeletal muscle mass
variables.why: The drug binds androgen receptor proteins in muscle and increases protein synthesis, causing hypertrophy.

why.correct: Excess androgen, and the estrogen made from it, closes the epiphyseal plates early, so adult height ends up lower. Some of the drug becomes estrogen and grows breast tissue. Acne is common. Feedback suppresses LH, so the testes shrink.
options: Correct. Estrogen made from the extra androgen matures and closes the plates early.
Early plate closure stops growth in length sooner, so adult height is lower, not higher.
Correct. Aromatase converts some of the drug to estrogen.
Feedback lowers LH, not raises it.
Correct. Androgens drive the skin's oil glands.
Correct. Without LH and FSH, the testes shrink.

why.correct: His testosterone is normal, yet his plates stay open. Without aromatase he makes almost no estrogen. So estrogen is the hormone that matures the plate cartilage and ends growth in length, in men as well as women.
options: If testosterone closed the plates, his normal testosterone would have closed them by his late teens.
Growth hormone drives growth at the plates; it does not close them.
Men's plates close too, normally by their early twenties, through estrogen made from testosterone. His stay open because he lacks that estrogen.
Correct. Estrogen closes the plates in both sexes.

why.correct: Thyroid hormones are needed for growth hormone to work at the epiphyseal plates and for bone to mature. A child who becomes hypothyroid slows in growth and falls behind in bone age, even with normal growth hormone.
options: At 7, sex hormones are still low in every child. A lack of them does not slow growth before puberty.
ADH controls how much water the kidneys keep. It has no role in bone growth.
Correct. Hypothyroidism slows growth and delays bone maturation.
Melatonin is a timing signal for the body clock and does not drive bone growth.

why.correct: In adults, red blood cells are made in the red bone marrow, and that is where EPO acts. The liver makes red blood cells only before birth.
options: This step is right. The kidney's tissue oxygen tracks what the blood can deliver.
This step is right. An oxygen-sensing protein that survives when oxygen is low switches on the EPO gene.
This is the error. EPO acts on the red bone marrow.
This step is right. More red cells enter the blood over days to weeks.
This step is right. Better oxygen delivery turns EPO back down: negative feedback.

why.correct: Stretch releases atrial natriuretic peptide (natri- = sodium, -uretic = relating to urine), which makes the kidneys excrete sodium and water.
options: Correct. ANP is the heart's hormone of stretch.
Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium, the opposite, and it comes from the adrenal cortex.
Erythropoietin comes from the kidney when oxygen is low and acts on red blood cell production.
Leptin comes from fat and signals the size of energy stores to the brain.

why.correct: The thymus is largest in childhood and grows until puberty. After that it slowly shrinks, and its working tissue is replaced by fat, so thymosin release falls with age.
options: Correct. The thymus shrinks and turns to fat after puberty.
The thymus grows only until about puberty.
The thymus stays in the mediastinum, behind the sternum, throughout life.
Melatonin comes from the pineal gland, not the thymus.

why.correct: EPO raised his red blood cell count, so his blood carried more oxygen but was also thicker. Losing plasma water by sweating concentrated the cells further. Thick blood flows poorly and clots more easily, raising the risk of stroke and heart attack.
options: EPO does not lower blood pressure; thicker blood, if anything, raises the resistance to flow.
Correct. Too many red blood cells plus too little plasma makes the blood thick and prone to clotting.
EPO acts on the bone marrow, not on the kidneys' handling of water.
EPO does not destroy platelets. The danger is clotting, not bleeding.
